content: The Heartland virus is a recently identified tick-borne virus belonging to the genus Phlebovirus and the family Bunyaviridae. It was first discovered in northwestern Missouri by Dr. Scott Folk at the Heartland Regional Medical Center in St. Joseph, Missouri. The virus was initially identified in humans in June 2009 when two farmers, living in separate locations, presented with symptoms including fever, fatigue, diarrhea, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), and leukopenia (low white blood cell count). The Heartland virus is part of the Bhanja virus serocomplex, and it is closely related to the Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) virus, which causes a similar illness and was recently discovered in China. Research conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Missouri Western State University has traced the virus to the Lone Star tick (Amblyomma americanum), which transmits the virus to humans during blood feeding. The Heartland virus is characterized by its genetic structure, consisting of three segments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA (-ssRNA). It is classified as a species within the Phlebovirus genus. Transmission of the Heartland virus occurs primarily through the bite of the Lone Star tick. In general, Phleboviruses can be transmitted by mosquitoes, ticks, and sandflies. All known cases of Heartland virus infection in the United States have involved patients who reported tick bites within the preceding 14 days. Symptoms of the infection include fever (≥100.4°F or 38°C), lethargy (weakness), headaches, myalgia (muscle pain), loss of appetite, nausea, diarrhea, weight loss, arthralgia (joint pain), leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Elevated liver transaminases may also be observed in affected individuals. Risk factors for Heartland virus infection include spending significant time outdoors in areas where ticks are endemic. All reported cases in the United States have occurred in three states: Missouri, Tennessee, and Oklahoma. Patients in these cases were all over the age of 50, and infections were reported between May and September. Diagnosis of Heartland virus infection is currently based on the exclusion of other infectious diseases with similar symptoms, such as ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis, or when patients fail to respond to treatment with the antibiotic doxycycline. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) can be used to detect viral RNA in the blood, and antibody titers against the virus may also indicate infection. Treatment for Heartland virus infection is supportive and non-specific, as antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections. Management typically involves intravenous fluid administration and medications to alleviate pain and other symptoms. Prevention of Heartland virus infection focuses on minimizing exposure to ticks. This includes using insect repellents on the skin and clothing, wearing long sleeves and pants to cover the body, and avoiding bushy or wooded areas where ticks are prevalent. After spending time outdoors, individuals should perform thorough tick checks and promptly remove any ticks found. When removing a tick, it is important to grasp it by the head rather than the abdomen, as squeezing the abdomen can force bacteria or viruses into the bite wound. Crushing an unattached tick can also release infectious agents from its abdomen, which may enter the skin or a wound.
